## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes procedures for recording weather and meteorological
conditions during field activities. Documenting weather conditions at
the time of sampling is essential for interpreting environmental data,
identifying storm-driven events, establishing baseline climate
conditions, and ensuring field safety. This SOP covers manual weather
observations, use of portable weather instruments, and deployment of
unattended data loggers for continuous monitoring.


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** All EA Program field activities where weather
  conditions may affect data interpretation, sample quality, or
  personnel safety; deployment and retrieval of portable weather
  stations and data loggers
- **Does not apply to:** Climate modeling or historical meteorological
  analysis; operation of fixed, permanently installed weather stations
  managed by other departments; air quality monitoring (see
  [SOP-F502](SOP-F502-air-quality-portable-sensors.qmd))
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Identify which weather variables are required for the
                      project; approve deployment of data loggers           |
| Trained Personnel | Record weather observations, deploy and retrieve
                      loggers, download data                               |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use                |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Lightning:** Cease all field activities and seek shelter in a
  vehicle or enclosed structure when lightning is observed. Wait at
  least 30 minutes after the last lightning strike before resuming.
- **Heat:** Southern California field sites can exceed 40 C. Carry
  adequate water, take shade breaks, and monitor for heat-related
  illness.
- **Wind:** High winds can topple tripod-mounted instruments and
  create hazardous conditions near exposed ridgelines or water bodies.
- **Flooding:** Rapidly changing weather can cause flash flooding in
  Southern California canyons and channels. Monitor upstream conditions
  and have an evacuation route planned.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen, long sleeves)
- [ ] Rain gear (if sampling during wet weather)
- [ ] Adequate water (minimum 1 L per person per 2 hours in hot
      conditions)

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd). For
lightning safety, follow the 30-30 rule: if the time between a flash
and thunder is 30 seconds or less, seek shelter; remain sheltered for
30 minutes after the last flash.


## 5. Equipment and Materials

### Manual Observation Equipment

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Sling psychrometer or digital hygrometer | For air temperature and relative humidity |
| Handheld anemometer (Kestrel or equivalent) | For wind speed and direction       |
| Manual rain gauge (graduated cylinder type) | For on-site precipitation measurement |
| Compass                               | For determining wind direction           |
| Cloud identification chart            | Laminated card for consistent sky observations |
| Field notebook                        | For recording all observations           |

### Portable Weather Stations and Data Loggers

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| HOBO MX series data logger (Onset)    | Temperature, relative humidity, light intensity |
| HOBO rain gauge (tipping bucket)      | For automated precipitation logging      |
| Tripod or mounting hardware           | For securing instruments at consistent height |
| Radiation shield (for temperature sensors) | Prevents direct solar heating of the sensor |
| Laptop or smartphone with HOBOconnect app | For programming loggers and downloading data |
| USB cable or Bluetooth adapter        | For data transfer                        |
| Spare batteries                       | Matched to logger model                  |
| Cable ties and ground stakes          | For securing equipment against wind      |


## 6. Procedure

### 6.1 Manual Weather Observations

Record the following observations at the start and end of every field
visit, and at the time of each sample collection. Enter all
observations in the field notebook per
[SOP-F003](SOP-F003-field-notebook-protocols.qmd).

| Variable                | Method                          | Units       |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------|:------------|
| Air temperature         | Sling psychrometer, Kestrel, or digital thermometer | C |
| Relative humidity       | Sling psychrometer or Kestrel   | %           |
| Wind speed              | Kestrel or Beaufort scale estimate | m/s or Beaufort number |
| Wind direction          | Compass bearing from which wind blows | degrees or cardinal direction |
| Cloud cover             | Visual estimate                 | Tenths (0--10) or oktas (0--8) |
| Cloud type              | Identify dominant type using chart | Name (e.g., cumulus, cirrus) |
| Precipitation           | Observation and rain gauge      | mm; also note type (rain, drizzle, none) |
| Barometric pressure (if available) | Kestrel or smartphone app | hPa or mbar |

::: {.callout-tip}
### Tip
If you do not have a weather instrument, still record qualitative
observations: "clear sky, calm winds, warm" is far better than nothing.
Note the source of any weather data you look up online (e.g., "NWS
Ontario station, 08:00 reading").
:::

### 6.2 Beaufort Wind Scale (Quick Reference)

| Beaufort | Description     | Speed (m/s) | Visual Indicator                |
|:---------|:----------------|:------------|:--------------------------------|
| 0        | Calm            | < 0.3       | Smoke rises vertically          |
| 1        | Light air       | 0.3--1.5    | Smoke drifts                    |
| 2        | Light breeze    | 1.6--3.3    | Leaves rustle                   |
| 3        | Gentle breeze   | 3.4--5.4    | Leaves and twigs in motion      |
| 4        | Moderate breeze | 5.5--7.9    | Small branches move; dust rises |
| 5        | Fresh breeze    | 8.0--10.7   | Small trees sway                |
| 6        | Strong breeze   | 10.8--13.8  | Large branches in motion        |

### 6.3 Deploying Portable Data Loggers

1. Select a deployment location that is representative of the site
   conditions and will not be disturbed by people, animals, or
   flooding.
2. Mount temperature and humidity loggers inside a radiation shield at
   a height of 1.5 m above ground level. Secure the shield to a
   tripod, post, or tree using cable ties.
3. Mount rain gauges on a level surface with no overhead obstructions
   (tree canopy, buildings). The gauge orifice should be
   approximately 1 m above ground.
4. Program the logger using the HOBOconnect app or HOBOware software:
   - Set the logging interval (typically 5 or 15 minutes for weather
     variables).
   - Set the start time (delayed start or immediate).
   - Confirm that the clock is synchronized to the correct time zone
     (Pacific Time).
5. Record the following in the field notebook:
   - Logger serial number
   - Deployment location (GPS coordinates per
     [SOP-F006](SOP-F006-gps-site-navigation.qmd))
   - Date and time of deployment
   - Logging interval
   - Sensor height above ground
6. Take a photograph of the deployed logger with surrounding context
   visible.

### 6.4 Retrieving Data from Loggers

1. Connect to the logger via Bluetooth (HOBOconnect) or USB cable
   (HOBOware).
2. Download the data and save the raw file using the naming convention:
   `YYYY-MM-DD_SiteID_LoggerSN_weather.csv`
3. Do not clear the logger memory until you have verified the
   downloaded file opens correctly and contains the expected date
   range.
4. If the logger is being left in the field, check the battery level
   and confirm the logging interval is still correct.
5. Upload the raw data file to the project GitHub repository under
   `data/weather/` within 48 hours.

### 6.5 Using Online Weather Data

When on-site instruments are not available, supplement field
observations with data from nearby weather stations. Preferred sources
for Southern California:

| Source                            | URL                                      |
|:----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| NWS (National Weather Service)    | <https://www.weather.gov>                |
| MesoWest / SynopticData          | <https://synopticdata.com/mesowest>      |
| CIMIS (California Irrigation Management Information System) | <https://cimis.water.ca.gov> |
| Weather Underground (personal stations) | <https://www.wunderground.com>     |

Record the station name, distance from field site, and retrieval date
in the field notebook and data file metadata.


## 7. Quality Control

- Cross-check manually recorded air temperature against the nearest
  reliable weather station (NWS or CIMIS). Discrepancies greater than
  3 C at similar elevation and time should be investigated.
- Inspect data loggers for drift by deploying two loggers side by side
  for at least 24 hours once per year. Temperature readings should
  agree within 0.5 C; humidity within 5%.
- Check rain gauge calibration at least once per year by pouring a
  known volume of water through the gauge and comparing the logged
  total to the expected value.
- Flag any suspicious data (e.g., sudden temperature jumps, constant
  humidity at 100% for days) during data review and note the issue in
  the project data log.

## 10. Training Record

Before recording weather observations or deploying loggers
independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Demonstrate correct use of a sling psychrometer or Kestrel meter
3. Demonstrate logger programming, deployment, and data download
   during a supervised field visit
4. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
